prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement B021 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not give me a new scientific reason, but it tested the old ones. The chain from incretin physiology and proglucagon processing, through the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and receptor biology, to drugs with large independent outcome trials, is the most complete on the shortlist. The mechanism is settled, the interpretation has been stable for decades, and recognition is timely. The identical opening ranks are not part of my argument. I also considered a second part and do not support one. No other achievement has clearly better credit than B021, so adding it would force a smaller B021 group and trade a defensible trio for a weaker pair or a contested trio. A single prize with a physiology-centred citation can be defended on its own terms.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Priority for the active truncated peptide is contested between Mojsov and the Habener group, and Habener is outside the credited names. I cannot settle this from the supplied record, and my recollection of the history is partly unverified. Keeping Knudsen out also means the prize honours the biology and not the step that produced the long-acting drugs. I would state this openly as a policy choice under the three-person cap. It is not a finding that her contribution was minor. If the Mojsov question cannot be resolved, a citation worded around the active form and not around who first identified it would be the minimum protection. CAR-T remains the strongest therapeutic alternative, and its Eshhar problem is not resolved by narrowing to June and Sadelain.

responses.point: Perlmann called Knudsen the most natural fourth name and said the three-person cap forces a choice. She would not displace Holst, Drucker or Mojsov, and she argued that rewarding translation would make the credit problem harder because industrial contributions were spread across many people.
responses.response: I agree with the last part and it settles the question for me. If translation were the criterion, the credit would spread across several programmes, and the cap would then force an arbitrary selection among industrial contributors, which I find harder to defend than leaving development out. I hold to my round-1 position and do not move Knudsen into the configuration. The citation must say clearly that it recognises the discoveries that enabled the therapies, so the omission reads as a deliberate line between physiology and development and not as an oversight. Your note that you did not rank B052 or B042 is fair. I still do not think either is ahead of the alternatives I name.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked B033 second but not as a clean attribution, because Eshhar's chimeric-receptor concept is outside the supplied names. He described a June and Sadelain pair as more defensible than adding Rosenberg, and a strong second part only if the committee accepts omitting that origin.
responses.response: I accept your correction that my pairing does not resolve the credit problem. It lowers the Rosenberg objection and leaves the Eshhar objection untouched. I do not think B033 should be the second part of this year's prize, because that would force a smaller B021 group and a contested CAR-T pair at the same time. I still keep it as my first alternative. If the committee ever moved away from B021 as the anchor, B033 is the achievement I would bring forward, but only with the Eshhar omission stated openly.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would keep the three academic names for B021 and said that any replacement for drug-development credit should rest on an explicit rationale and not on default. She also raised long-term safety, secondary malignancy and activity beyond haematological cancers as reasons to narrow or wait on CAR-T, and asked whether B032 deserves renewed consideration as a second part.
responses.response: I agree that any substitution should be argued explicitly, and I see no rationale in the record that justifies dropping Holst, Drucker or Mojsov. On CAR-T maturity I now give your concern more weight than in round 1. Durable benefit in B-cell malignancy is established, but the evidence on secondary malignancy and solid tumours is still incomplete, which strengthens my reluctance to build a two-part prize on it. On B032, the attribution to Feldmann and Maini is cleaner than for B021, and I do not read the long record as a weakness. My reservation is the same as the others raised against it, namely how much of the discovery is TNF biology and antibody engineering done by others. I would not support it as a second part, and I would not rank it above B033 or B044.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied record settles the Mojsov and Habener priority for the active GLP-1 peptide. I do not think it does, and a citation that avoids a priority claim is the safeguard.
Whether the line that leaves out Knudsen and industrial development is the right policy, or only the easiest one under the three-person cap.
Whether any split of the six optogenetics names can be defended without misrepresenting priority.
How the CAR-T attribution should be handled given Eshhar's absence from the supplied names, and whether the long-term safety record is mature enough.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented tie to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My documented link to spatial transcriptomics and brain atlases does not connect to the shortlist. Sandberg has disclosed that we co-authored papers and share Karolinska Institutet. Neither of us is a candidate, and I do not read this as a recusal issue.
